governingDotPoints.text: Use partitioning and place value to multiply 2-, 3- and 4-digit numbers by one-digit numbers

topic.title: Multiplicative relations A
topic.blurb: Products, factors, multiplication and division strategies.

scope.decision: earliest applicable course/topic in skill.stage; confirm against title, blurb and prerequisites
scope.stage3Borrowing: Later-stage booklet wording/presentation only; mathematics, assumed knowledge and terminology remain Stage 3

theory.intro: You can multiply a large number by splitting it into its place-value parts, multiplying each part, then adding. This is the **distributive property**.
facts: Multiply **each part** by the multiplier, then add the part-products.
Include the thousands when partitioning a 4-digit number. A zero part gives a product of $0$, so it need not have a rectangle in the area model.
If the part-products and one factor are known, divide each part-product by that factor, then add the parts to find the missing factor.
steps: Partition the larger number by place value.
Multiply each part by the other factor.
Add the part-products to get the total.

workedExamples.solution_text:
The place-value parts are $200$, $60$ and $7$.
$200\times4=800$
$60\times4=240$
$7\times4=28$
$267\times4=800+240+28=1068$.
For the different partition, $267=260+7$.
$260\times4=1040$ and $7\times4=28$.
$1040+28=1068$. Both partitions give the same product.

$1406=1000+400+0+6$.
$1000\times7=7000$
$400\times7=2800$
$6\times7=42$
$1406\times7=7000+2800+42=9842$.
The tens part is $0$, and $0\times7=0$. It adds nothing to the product, so the model has only the three nonzero parts.

workedExamples.question_text: The part-products for $\square\times8$ are $2400$, $560$ and $48$. Find the missing factor and check the total product.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Divide each part-product by the known factor $8$.
$2400\div8=300$
$560\div8=70$
$48\div8=6$
The missing factor is $300+70+6=376$.
Check: $376\times8=2400+560+48=3008$.

mastery.question_text: Without changing the product, partition $247$ in a different way from $200+40+7$, then calculate $247 \times 6$.

A student writes $503 \times 8=(500 \times 8)+(30 \times 8)$.
Explain the error and find the correct product.

Complete the equality: $326 \times 7=(300 \times 7)+(20 \times 7)+(\square \times 7)$.
Then find the product.

options.why: Used the tens digit 3 instead of its value 30, so the parts add to 7 rather than 34.
Gave the ones digit 4 a tens value of 40, so the parts add to 70 rather than 34.
Used $3$ ones and $4$ tens, representing $43$ rather than $34$.
Added 7 and 8 instead of multiplying the side lengths.
Used $6\times8$ instead of the labelled $7\times8$.
Attached an extra zero to the ones part-product.
The hundreds part alone is $100\times5=500$, so $460$ cannot be the total.
Calculated the hundreds part as 400 instead of 500.
Used $5$ instead of $15$ for $3\times5$, giving $500+400+5=905$.
Dropped a place-value zero, multiplying 40 by 7 instead of 400 by 7.
Read the 6 ones as 60, multiplying 60 by 7 instead of 6 by 7.
Shifted both parts one place: used 40 for the hundreds part and 60 for the ones part.

questions.question_text:
The part-products for $\square \times 4$ are $1200$, $80$ and $12$.
What number is in the box?

options.why: Added the part-products to find the total product, not the missing factor.
Reversed the tens and ones quotients when rebuilding the factor.
$308\times4=1232$, which does not match the total $1200+80+12=1292$.

questions.question_text:
A student calculates $274 \times 3$ as $600+210+12$.
Which statement is correct?

options.why: Dropped a zero from the hundreds part-product.
Used the digit 7 instead of its place value 70.
Added the ones digit and multiplier instead of multiplying them.

questions.question_text: Which different partition can be used to calculate $156 \times 4$ without using $100+50+6$?

options.why: Dropped the zero from 150, so the parts total 21 instead of 156.
Read the ones digit 6 as 60, so the parts total 210 instead of 156.
Shifted both parts one place, using 15 tens as 15 and 6 ones as 60.

methods.description: Partition a positive whole-number factor into place-value parts (or regroup adjoining parts without changing their sum), multiply each part by the one-digit factor and add the part-products. Include thousands when present; omit zero-area parts. Use the same calculations to fill/check parts and diagnose a wrong partition or product.

When the one-digit factor and its partial products are given, divide each product by that known factor, add the recovered place-value parts, and check by multiplying. This is an inverse use of the Stage 3 area multiplication-and-division context, not an added long-division algorithm.

preparedSources.excerpt:
- Use informal written strategies such as the area model to solve
  multiplication and division problems

+------------------------------------------------------------------+
|**Example(s):**|
||
|Such as $$8 \times 27$$.|
||
|![2 area model diagrams showing 8 times 27. Details in text|
|below diagram.](media/image9.png){width="3.6949682852143484in"|
|height="1.6666666666666667in"}|
||
|(area model).\|
|*Image long description*: The area model partitions 27 into its|
|place values, 20 and 7, to break down the equation into 2|
|simpler equations, 20 times 8 (160) and 7 times 8 (56). The|
|answers to these simpler equations are added to get a final|
|answer of 216.|
+------------------------------------------------------------------+

- Use the distributive property with the area model to partition numbers
  in representing multiplication problems

+------------------------------------------------------------------+
|**Example(s):**|
||
|Such as $$684 \times 5$$.|
||
|![Area model of 684 partitioned into its place values to solve|
|684 times 5. Details|
|below.](media/image10.png){width="2.6650568678915136in"|
|height="1.6666666666666667in"}|
||
|(area model).\|
|*Image long description:* The area model partitions 684 into its|
|place values, 600, 80 and 4 to break down the equation into 2|
|simpler equations, 600 times 5 (3000), 80 times 5 (400) and 4|
|times 5 (20). The answers to these simpler equations are added|
|to get a final answer of 3420.|
+------------------------------------------------------------------+

- Use the distributive property with partial products to solve problems
  by multiplying the hundreds, then the tens and then the ones

+------------------------------------------------------------------+
|**Example(s):**|
||
|Such as|
|$$684 \times 3 = (600 \times 3) + (80 \times 3) + (4 \times 3)$$|
||
|$$= 1800 + 240 + 12$$|
||
|$$= 2052$$|
+------------------------------------------------------------------+
